A pair of stick-back chairs reputed to have been made by Jimmy Possum — the legs run through the slab seat to support the arms. Tasmanian School of Art catalogue, 1978.
The Small Greenhill Chair (exhibit 2) by George Greenhill, in reclaimed timber and house paint. Photo: Lewis Laskin, QVMAG, 2022.
Rive radially — halve through the pith, quarter, then split billets along the rays. Shave downhill, with the grain.
Red oak (left) and white oak (right) — both make fine chairs. Alexander, Make a Chair from a Tree.
Score pith-to-bark, start a wedge, then leap-frog wedges along the opening crack.
Seat the froe in the end grain with the club; lever the handle to open and steer the split.
You sit astride the horse, clamp the work with your feet, and draw the knife toward you.
The four stages: rough riven billet, two adjacent faces, four-square, octagon.
An antique Jimmy Possum with its original paint — note the broad slab seat and the raked stance. Photo: Lewis Laskin, QVMAG, 2022.
Scribe a line 1.5 in from each edge; a hole sits where two lines meet at a corner.
Clamp the arms UNDER the seat, centerlines on the side layout lines, and bore both at once.
Jam the rounded top, mark two lines, shape the tenon between them, seat it.
Side view: legs rake through the seat; the back leg's foot lands well behind it.
An antique Jimmy Possum seen from below — the legs run straight through the slab seat to meet the arms. Photo: Lewis Laskin, QVMAG, 2022.
Stand the chair on a flat surface, shim it, and scribe each leg to one height.
Assemble — and disassemble — in the order the chair was built.
A white-oak-and-walnut Jimmy Possum of my own — the through-tenons stand proud and wedged. Photo: Lewis Laskin.
Coarse to fine: hog out with an adze or gouge, refine with a scorp, smooth with a travisher, finish with a scraper.
A walnut Jimmy Possum chair I built, on show at Maryland Hall. Photo: Lewis Laskin.
The Roy Larcombe Chair, c.1900 (exhibit 18). Photo: Lewis Laskin, QVMAG.
Another antique example — the raked legs and legs-through-seat joinery are unmistakable. Photo: Lewis Laskin, QVMAG.
